title: Quickstart Templates — User Interviews Notes + Synthesis (Early adopters + Solutions Eng)
content:
Context
- Goal: understand where onboarding breaks for RAG + agent templates, what users mean by “production-ready,” and which template defaults/features drive adoption vs create friction.
- Participants: mix of early adopters (self-serve PLG users + friendly customers) and internal Solutions Engineering (SE) / Support perspectives.
- Method: 30–45 min semi-structured interviews, plus follow-up via Slack/email when we needed logs/screenshots.
- Note: Names below are anonymized unless internal (SE/Support). Company names are omitted; we reference segments (startup, mid-market SaaS, regulated/enterprise) and common patterns.

Interview guide (used loosely)
1) First 30 minutes: “Try to get from signup to the template running locally.” Where do you stall?
2) What does production-ready mean for your org? Which checkboxes matter most?
3) What templates would you actually ship to prod? What would you never ship?
4) What is your preferred deployment target (serverless, container, k8s, VPC)?
5) Observability: what do you need on day 1 vs later?
6) Security: secrets, PII, audit, data retention.
7) How do you want updates/upgrades to work?

Participants (summary)
- External / early adopters
  A1: AI startup engineer (TypeScript, Next.js + Node backend).
  A2: Mid-market SaaS platform engineer (Python, FastAPI, k8s).
  A3: Mid-market SaaS app engineer (Python, prefers minimal infra; wants “works on laptop” path).
  A4: Regulated customer engineer (Private/VPC interest; security/audit heavy).
  A5: Solutions architect (consultant integrator) building POCs across providers; anti-lock-in.
- Internal
  SE1: Solutions Engineering (frequent RAG pilots, enterprise evals).
  SE2: Solutions Engineering (platform/infra heavy customers).
  SUP1: Support (top onboarding tickets for hosted API).

Topline synthesis (TL;DR)
- “Production-ready” is less about fancy agent features and more about: predictable failure modes + observability + safe defaults + deployment story.
- Most common onboarding breakpoints:
  (1) API key + environment variable confusion (where to put it, .env vs shell, errors not actionable)
  (2) Streaming + proxies (disconnects, partial responses, retry semantics)
  (3) Vector store / retrieval setup (users want a no-infra local path, but also a clear upgrade path)
  (4) OTel collector setup (people want “it works with no collector” and “it works with my existing collector”)
  (5) Rate limits / 429s (templates accidentally encourage concurrency that triggers 429 for self-serve)
- Template must-haves (users repeatedly asked for these):
  - A “doctor” command or equivalent preflight checks
  - Minimal, local-first default (no external DB required to demo RAG)
  - Strong error messages with copy/paste remediation
  - Cost controls: explicit max_tokens + timeouts + bounded retries + concurrency guidance
  - Traceability: request_id in logs, consistent trace/span attributes, and a quick way to confirm telemetry is working
  - A clear deployment story (Docker is the baseline; k8s optional but valued)
- Users are OK with opinionated defaults IF we explain them and provide “how to tune” sections.

What users mean by “production-ready” (ranked)
1) Reliability / resilience
   - Timeout defaults that prevent hung requests.
   - Retries with jitter/backoff that don’t amplify outages.
   - Circuit breaker behavior or at least “stop retrying forever.”
   - Streaming robustness (resume/reconnect strategy or safe failure semantics).
2) Observability
   - Traces that show: request → retrieval → model → tools → response.
   - Metrics they can alert on: latency, error rate, tool failure rate, retrieval empty/low-hit rate, token usage.
   - Log fields: request_id / correlation_id, model, status_code, error_type, latency, token counts.
3) Security / compliance basics
   - No secrets in logs. No printing env by default.
   - PII guidance and redaction patterns.
   - Safe defaults around storing prompts/responses.
4) Deployment + operations
   - Dockerfile and “one command run” locally.
   - k8s manifests for serious teams.
   - Config via env (12-factor). 
   - Version pinning: model and template version captured.
5) Maintainability
   - Tests (even smoke tests) and a clear upgrade path.

Detailed notes by interview

A1 (AI startup, TS stack)
- Goal: ship a RAG-powered support assistant quickly; wants TS template first.
- Biggest friction:
  - Streaming errors are hard to interpret. They see “socket hang up” / fetch aborts and don’t know if it’s Redwood, their proxy, or Node.
  - Tool calling: “I don’t care about agent buzzwords; I care that tool calls don’t silently fail.”
- Production-ready to them:
  - A known-good default model + pinned version; ability to swap later.
  - A “safe mode” that returns a non-streaming response when streaming fails.
- Quote: “If the quickstart teaches the wrong retry behavior, we’ll copy it everywhere and regret it.”
- Asks:
  - Provide a single “recommended” TS client init pattern.
  - Provide a troubleshooting section specifically for streaming behind proxies.

A2 (Platform engineer, Python/FastAPI, k8s)
- Goal: standardize inference access across teams; cares about observability integration.
- Biggest friction:
  - OTel collector: they already have one; they don’t want to run another local collector just to try the template.
  - Wants explicit span naming and low-cardinality attributes. Worried about user_id / prompt hashes in attributes.
- Production-ready:
  - “If it emits good traces/metrics out of the box and doesn’t blow up cardinality, that’s 80%.”
  - Wants dashboards or at least metric names aligned to something they can wire quickly.
- Quote: “Don’t ship a demo that can’t be put under an SLO.”
- Asks:
  - Provide two observability modes: (1) local dev (optional collector) (2) bring-your-own collector (env-only config).
  - Document which attributes are stable contracts vs best-effort.

A3 (App engineer, Python, minimal infra)
- Goal: validate RAG quality fast; doesn’t want to learn vector DBs on day 1.
- Biggest friction:
  - Retrieval pipeline complexity is overwhelming. They want to point to a folder of docs and go.
  - Chunking defaults: asked “why these numbers?”
- Production-ready:
  - A “good enough” local index to prove it works.
  - Clear knobs: top_k, chunk_size, overlap, max_context_tokens.
- Quote: “I need an obvious path: folder → index → ask question. Anything else is a distraction.”
- Asks:
  - Make “ingest my docs” the first-class path.
  - Provide a “what to tune first” section and a mini eval script.

A4 (Regulated/enterprise, Private/VPC oriented)
- Goal: evaluate Redwood Private; wants template as reference implementation for internal governance.
- Biggest friction:
  - Wants logging redaction defaults and explicit guidance on what not to log.
  - Wants separation of control plane vs data plane explained in template docs (even if brief).
- Production-ready:
  - Audit-friendly logs, deterministic config, and a sane baseline for incident response (error taxonomy).
  - Prefer non-telemetry by default (or explicit opt-in), especially anything that adds headers.
- Quote: “A template is a security artifact. People will copy it verbatim.”
- Asks:
  - Provide a section: “Running in regulated environments (VPC/private)” and “PII do’s/don’ts.”
  - Avoid hidden network calls / analytics without opt-in.

A5 (Integrator/consultant, anti-lock-in)
- Goal: build POCs across multiple providers; wants abstraction.
- Biggest friction:
  - Templates often entangle provider-specific response formats and error handling.
- Production-ready:
  - A clean provider interface + model config separation.
  - Clear “swap the LLM provider” guide.
- Quote: “Don’t say ‘provider-agnostic’ if the whole codebase assumes one chat schema.”
- Asks:
  - Keep the Redwood-specific pieces in a thin adapter layer.

SE1 (Solutions Engineering)
- Observed pattern: “Time-to-first-success” fails because users don’t know what ‘success’ looks like.
  - They need a single command that prints:
    - model used
    - request_id
    - latency
    - tokens
    - a sample trace link or at least “trace exported: yes/no”
- Biggest friction seen in the field:
  - 401/403 confusion (wrong key, wrong env var name, wrong region/base URL).
  - 429 due to template concurrency defaults.
  - Corporate proxies blocking unknown headers; telemetry header issues.
- Quote: “Give them a doctor command before you give them more features.”

SE2 (Solutions Engineering, platform-heavy customers)
- Wants clear separation between:
  - “reference architecture” (what we recommend)
  - “template implementation details” (what can be swapped)
- Biggest friction:
  - People don’t know which metrics matter. They ship without alerts.
- Asks:
  - Include recommended alerts/SLOs but caution about noisy defaults.
  - Include cost dashboards or at least token cost breakdown.

SUP1 (Support)
- Top ticket clusters related to quickstarts/examples today:
  1) streaming disconnects (proxy / load balancer)
  2) OTel exporter misconfig (endpoint/auth) 
  3) 429 + lack of backoff 
  4) tool schema parse errors / unclear error messages
- Quote: “Most tickets are ‘it didn’t work’ with no context. If templates emitted the right logs, half of these would be solved in one reply.”

Common onboarding breakpoints (concrete)
1) Environment variables / config
- Users forget to export env vars; .env isn’t loaded; multiple names for the same thing.
- They want a single source of truth (e.g., TEMPLATE_CONFIG env schema) and validation that tells them exactly what is missing.
- Strong preference for:
  - “copy .env.example → .env”
  - clear required vs optional sections
  - a validator that fails fast before running the server

2) Streaming stability
- Failure mode: proxy closes idle connections; streaming aborts; users see partial tokens.
- Users want clear behavior:
  - When do we retry?
  - If we retry, do we risk duplicate outputs?
  - Can we fall back to non-streaming for reliability?
- Request: include a section “Running behind proxies (nginx, corporate proxies, cloud load balancers).”

3) Retrieval complexity / vector store choice
- Many want local-first retrieval. They don’t want to choose a hosted vector DB up front.
- But platform teams want at least one “real” adapter path.
- Repeated ask: “Start with local; document upgrade path to hosted.”

4) Observability setup
- People like that we use OTel, but they do not like needing to stand up a collector to see anything.
- Ask: allow console logging traces in dev or noop exporter by default.
- Need a single “verify observability” step: run script → prints “traces exported OK” and where.

5) Rate limiting / cost
- Default concurrency should not cause immediate 429 for self-serve.
- Users asked for explicit “cost guardrails” section with:
  - max_tokens default
  - max iterations for agent loop
  - tool output size limits
  - concurrency limit
  - caching notes (if applicable)

Template must-haves (requirements we should treat as launch blockers)
- Preflight validation (CLI doctor or built-in check): missing env vars, API reachability, collector reachability.
- Error taxonomy in logs: network/auth/quota/tool/retrieval/validation.
- request_id propagation into logs and (if possible) trace attributes.
- A minimal ingestion path: “point at folder → run ingest → ask.”
- Safe defaults: timeouts, bounded retries, backoff, max_tokens, agent max_iterations.
- Troubleshooting: 401/429/streaming disconnect/collector config/tool schema errors.

Nice-to-haves (not blockers, but high leverage)
- A simple eval harness (golden prompts) that runs in CI and locally.
- Deployment recipes (Fly.io/Render) for startups; k8s for platform teams.
- A guide for provider swapping / abstraction.

Action items (rolling)
- Docs / DevEx
  - Add explicit “What success looks like” section to template README: expected output, sample logs, where to find request_id.
  - Add “Streaming behind proxies” troubleshooting page + recommended settings.
  - Add “Tune these 5 knobs first” for RAG: chunk size, overlap, top_k, max_context_tokens, reranker on/off.
- Engineering
  - Implement/strengthen config schema + validation utilities shared across templates (ref: ENG-4187).
  - Ensure default concurrency + retries do not trigger 429 for typical free-tier limits (align with safe defaults policy).
  - Make telemetry tagging opt-in; document corporate proxy issues and how to disable headers.
  - Add observability verification script / command (ties into OTel integration work).
- Support enablement
  - Update troubleshooting to request specific fields: request_id, error_type, status_code, exporter endpoint, proxy info.

Open questions
- How much should templates “phone home” for adoption metrics? Strong preference is opt-in; at minimum, no sensitive headers by default.
- What is the minimal cross-provider abstraction we can support without making the template too abstract?
- For streaming retry: do we standardize on “no automatic retry mid-stream” (to avoid duplication), or a best-effort reconnect? Users want clarity more than magic.

Appendix: raw quotes (sanitized)
- “If I can’t understand the error in 30 seconds, I’m going back to my old codebase.”
- “A template should feel like a reference service with guardrails, not a blog tutorial.”
- “Please don’t teach my team to log prompts by default.”
- “I want to see one trace and immediately understand where time went: retrieval vs model vs tool.”

Appendix: what we should measure (from interviews)
- Time-to-first-success: time from ‘template init’ to first successful response.
- Template retention: do they still run the template 7/30 days later?
- Support deflection: reduction in 401/429/streaming tickets when users adopt templates.
- Observability adoption: % templates with traces/metrics enabled (even if to local collector).

(End of doc — add new interview notes above the synthesis section and update synthesis monthly.)
